cards.h: A city smaller than a dust grain
cards.b:
Every cell is like a tiny city. It has a wall or border, power plants, factories, a library, a post office and a waste team. Once you know the parts, diseases, antibiotics and even cancer start to make sense.

There are two big city plans: the simple one (prokaryote) and the planned, walled-room one (eukaryote).

Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) have no nucleus. DNA floats in a region called the nucleoid. Eukaryotes (animals, plants, fungi, protists) keep DNA in a membrane-bound nucleus and have many membrane-bound organelles.

The nucleus holds DNA and is wrapped by a double membrane with pores. Inside, the nucleolus builds ribosome parts. Robert Brown named the nucleus in 1831. Instructions are copied here as messenger RNA and sent out through the pores.

cards.h: Ribosomes, ER and Golgi: factory and post office
cards.b: Ribosomes are the protein makers. The rough ER (studded with ribosomes) makes proteins for export; the smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies. The Golgi (found by Camillo Golgi, 1898) sorts and packs them.

Mitochondria make most of the cell's ATP, the energy currency. They have their own DNA and double membrane. Lynn Margulis (1967) argued they were once free bacteria swallowed by a bigger cell: the endosymbiotic theory. Chloroplasts have a similar story.

Lysosomes hold enzymes that digest worn-out parts, like the recycling unit.
Plant cells also have a cellulose cell wall, a large central vacuole for water and storage, and chloroplasts for photosynthesis. Animal cells have centrioles for division and no wall.

A web of protein fibres gives shape and lets the cell move. Microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules act as scaffolding and rails for transport. Cilia and flagella are built from microtubules.

Hooke used a microscope in 1665. Anton van Leeuwenhoek saw living bacteria in the 1670s. The electron microscope, built by Ernst Ruska in 1931, revealed organelles far too small for light. Albert Claude and later George Palade used spinning (centrifugation) to separate parts and study them.

Common errors

  • Bacteria are not 'primitive and simple' in chemistry; they are very successful.
  • Mitochondria are not 'powerhouses making energy from nothing'; they convert food energy into ATP.
  • Red blood cells in humans lose the nucleus, so not every eukaryotic cell has one.

The Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, and the National Centre for Cell Science, Pune, study cell biology. G.N. Ramachandran at Madras, in 1954, worked out the triple-helix structure of collagen, a key protein outside cells. Ramachandran plots are still used to check protein shapes.

• Prokaryotes lack a nucleus; eukaryotes have one plus organelles.
  • Protein path: ribosome, ER, Golgi, vesicle.
  • Mitochondria and chloroplasts likely came from engulfed bacteria.
  • Plant cells add wall, vacuole, chloroplast.

Think about it:

  1. Why might cells with high energy needs, like muscle, have more mitochondria?
  2. What clue suggests mitochondria were once bacteria?
